R0267.title: Physical-World Prompt Injection Attack
R0267.definition: An adversarial attack where the attacker places visual cues (stickers, printed patterns, occluders, projections) in the physical environment of an embodied-intelligence robot to induce its Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model to misperceive or execute unintended actions.
R0267.description:
Physical-world prompt injection inherits from indirect prompt injection of large language models, but in embodied-intelligence scenarios the consequence escalates from information leakage to physical-world dangerous actions. The attacker needs no contact with the robot or training-data poisoning; merely placing a written instruction, a specific pattern, or projected light in the environment may cause the VLM to treat it as a user instruction. The CHAI (Command Hijacking against embodied AI) research measured this across drone emergency landing, autonomous driving, and aerial target tracking scenarios, with attack success rates significantly higher than prior methods, capable of causing a drone to land improperly or crash. The Shawshank indirect-jailbreak framework induces embodied AI to perform harmful behaviors via malicious environmental instructions (e.g., wall text), breaching all tested VLMs.

This risk is a core threat distinguishing embodied intelligence from pure software AI — the injectioncarrier resides in the physical world, so pure input filtering cannot eradicate it, and consequences translate directly into physical actions. It belongs to the model-layer attack family together with R0271 (VLA/VLM adversarial attack), but this risk focuses on physical-environment injectioncarrier, while the latter focuses on digital adversarial examples and jailbreaks.
R0267.influence: Can induce robots to perform dangerous actions (e.g., unlocking, transporting contraband, striking people), leak environment information, or bypass safety constraints; because the injectioncarrier is in the physical world, it is hard to eradicate via pure software filtering, with low attack threshold yet high harm.

references.title: CHAI: Command Hijacking against embodied AI

observables: Unexpected text stickers, printed patterns, or projections appear in robot operating environments
VLA models execute dangerous actions inconsistent with the task when specific visual cues appear
Drones or autonomous devices unexpectedly land or turn at specific locations
Newly added adversarial stickers in the environment correlate temporally with robot anomalous behavior
Robot logs show environmental text or patterns being executed as user commands
